# How the Course Works

The course runs on a **dual spine**. Every week pairs:

- **A workflow concept, taught hands-on in class.** Our 2.5-hour weekly session is
  a workshop. We learn a workflow skill by *doing it together* in real time — the
  first time you make a repository, open a pull request, or set up continuous
  integration, you'll do it live in class.
- **An ambitious take-home build.** Each week's individual assignment is a
  build in an unfamiliar domain that forces you to apply that week's workflow
  skill on your own, at higher stakes. Every build includes a short **reading**
  that connects the work to the bigger picture.

The semester has two parts:

- **Part 1: Working with an agent (Meetings 1–8).** We start with Git *by hand*,
  look under the hood at how LLMs work and fail, and then climb a trust gradient:
  high-touch collaboration with an agent → leverage (skills) → delegating work and
  verifying it → automating verification with continuous integration.
- **Part 2: Building with LLMs (Meetings 9–12).** We apply the workflow to real
  data analysis in Python, call LLMs from your own code with chatlas, connect
  agents to tools with MCP, and orchestrate multiple agents.

From Meeting 9 on, the last ~45 minutes of each class is **team studio time** for
your team project. The semester ends with two dedicated studio meetings and final
presentations during the final exam slot. See the [schedule](schedule.qmd) for the
meeting-by-meeting plan.

# Assignments

## Participation & Attendance

**Attendance will be taken and is the primary driver of your participation grade.**

In-class work is hands-on and ungraded — but it is *practice for the build you do
at home*. The take-home builds assume the skills we develop together in class, so
missing class costs you twice: once on participation, and again on a much harder
homework. Plan to attend in person every week.

## Individual Builds

There are **11 builds**, each an ambitious project in a domain you likely haven't
worked in before. Each build is delivered as a **GitHub repository that includes
the full conversation history** with the agent, plus a short reflection on the
build's assigned reading. Grading focuses on prompt quality, evidence of iterative
collaboration, final product quality, and thoughtful use of the week's workflow
skill. Builds are graded with a checklist, you may **resubmit once** for a revised
score, and your **lowest build score is dropped**.

## Oral Code Walkthroughs

Twice during the semester you'll spend 5–10 minutes in class walking the instructor
through one of your builds: how it works, and *why you (or the agent) did it that
way*. The goal is durable learning. If you can't explain what the agent built, you
don't yet own it.

## Team Project

Throughout the semester you'll work in **teams of 3–4** on an open-ended project of
your own design — the one piece of fully open-ended work in the course. It is
broken into milestone deliverables (proposal, interim report, final report,
presentation). See the [project overview](project/0-overview.qmd) for details.

# Grading

Final grades will be calculated as follows:

<div style="width:650px">

Item | Weight | Notes
-----|--------|----------------------------------
Individual Builds (11) | 40% | Lowest dropped; 10 builds × 4%; one resubmission allowed
Oral Code Walkthroughs (2) | 10% | 2 × 5%, in class
Team Project: Proposal | 5% | Teams of 3–4 (Oct 14)
Team Project: Interim Report | 10% | (Nov 18)
Team Project: Final Report | 15% | (Dec 7)
Final Presentation | 10% | (Final exam slot)
Participation / Attendance | 10% | Yes, attendance is taken

</div>

## AI Tools and Cost

You'll need an AI coding agent for this course, and the most economical option is a
**subscription of about $20/month**:

- **[Claude Pro](https://claude.ai/login?plan=pro)** (for Claude Code), or
- **[ChatGPT Plus](https://chatgpt.com/pricing)** (for Codex).

Choose one. You're welcome to use a different agentic coding tool instead (e.g.,
Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot, OpenCode), since the underlying skills transfer, but
in-class instruction will use Claude Code and Codex.

**Why a subscription and not the API?** Agentic coding burns a lot of tokens.
Paying per token through an API would cost *far* more than a flat monthly
subscription. We recommend a subscription for exactly that reason. I recognize that
$20/month is a real cost. We are pursuing institutional access, so check Slack
before you pay, and let me know if the cost is a barrier.

**API access for Meetings 10–11.** A subscription does not include API access, and
we'll call LLMs from Python code with [chatlas](https://posit-dev.github.io/chatlas/)
in those meetings. You can do this at no cost with a free-tier or local model, or by
loading about **$5** of credit on a provider's API and using a small model. The
course materials work with any provider. We'll go over the options in class before
Meeting 10.

## Generative-AI Use Policy

Using AI agents is not "cheating" in this course — **it is the core skill being
taught.** Using the language of the
[MIT report on AI and education](https://aiandeducation.mit.edu/report/), the policy
for individual builds is **required use of generative AI**: you must use an agentic
coding tool and submit your full conversation history. You remain fully responsible
for the correctness, quality, and originality of everything you submit: read what
the agent produces, run it, and fix it when it's wrong.

There are two **AI-free exceptions**, each with a reason:

- **Meeting 1 and Build 1 (Git by hand).** You can't supervise an agent that uses
  Git until you can use Git yourself.
- **Reading reflections.** These are written in your own words, because the point is
  your own thinking about the reading.

Other course commitments:

- **No AI detectors.** We do not use AI-detection software, which is unreliable.
  The evidence of your process is your conversation logs and your Git history.
- **Instructor disclosure.** I use AI in preparing course materials and in drafting
  grading feedback, and I review everything before you see it.
- **Log privacy.** Conversation logs are seen only by the course staff and used only
  for grading. Remove API keys, passwords, and personal data from your logs before
  you submit them.
- **Responsible use.** We'll discuss failure modes, ethics, environmental cost, and
  when *not* to use AI throughout the course.

Detailed disclosure requirements appear in each assignment.
